newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany faces new unemployment blow-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Germany faces new unemployment blow-analysts.

text.p: Germany's jobs crisis will intensify this week when new data show a jump in unemployment to over four million for the first time since last winter, while the underlying trend continues to climb, analysts said on Tuesday.

Germany's DGB trade union federation sounded the alarm bells, warning that unadjusted December unemployment would rise to 4.1 million before climbing to a post-war record of between 4.5 and 4.6 million by February.
Economists polled by Reuters before Thursday's release of data for December expect no break in the upward trend in adjusted unemployment, which strips out seasonal factors.
They predicted a rise of between 35,000 and 60,000 from November's record 4.1 million.
"The trend will remain unbroken," economist Thomas Mayer at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt told Reuters.
A combination of unspectacular economic growth, aggressive downsizing by German firms and a second successive bone-chilling winter will swell dole queues to a point last seen in the 1930s.
With no sign of a turnaround in the jobs market, economists say that a government goal of halving unemployment by the turn of the century has slipped out of reach.

The influential DIW research institute, one of six whose forecasts underpin government policy, said the current recovery was the weakest since the war and that the government had done too little, too late to create new jobs.
"The longer it takes to achieve a sweeping change in the labour market, the less likely is it that the government will meet its goal of halving unemployment by the year 2000," DIW said in a report.
DIW cut its 1997 growth forecast to two percent from 2.5 percent and said unemployment would peak at 4.5 million.
Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt, who only last month reaffirmed the jobs target, has become the latest government minister to distance himself from it.

"I am very worried that there has been no improvement in the labour market despite the positive development of the economy recently," he said this week. "Against this background it will be hard to halve unemployment in the next three years."

Unemployment has also been the Achilles heel in Finance Minister Theo Waigel's bid to slash spending and borrowing so that Germany meets the tight fiscal limits this year set by the Maastricht treaty to join European monetary union in 1999.

DGB deputy head Ursula Engelen-Kefer, who also sits on the board of the Federal Labour Office which calculates jobless data, said on Tuesday she expected unemployment to average 4.1 million this year.

That is well over the official forecast underlying Waigel's 1997 austerity budget designed to reduce state borrowing below the three percent limit of gross domestic product specified by the Maastricht treaty.
Higher unemployment hampers that goal in two ways, by reducing government tax revenues and boosting outlays for jobless benefits.

Most economists agreed with the DIW prediction that Germany would overshoot the deficit goal -- significant because both Waigel and top Bundesbank officials insist on a strict reading of the Maastricht treaty.
"Waigel's prediction has always been too optimistic," said Stephen King at HSBC James Capel in London. He sees the deficit at 3.3 percent.
How soon the budget arithmetic may unravel is unclear, but Mayer said the situation would become clear by the time of the next European Union summit in Holland this summer.
"The moment of truth will come in Amsterdam in June. Only then will we find out whether monetary union can go ahead as planned or whether there will be a delay," Mayer said.
